sections.h2: What should Livingston, NJ sellers focus on first?
sections.html:
Livingston is a high-value Essex County township, so the biggest costs in a sale are usually the price-based state fees and any repairs a buyer's inspector flags. The local paperwork is short: a smoke detector certification from the fire department and a check for open building permits. What remains is the deed, the state's fee tables and the Essex County recording office.

Livingston covers 13.79 square miles of land, and the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 32,223 residents. Its 2020 count of 31,330 was the highest the township has recorded.

sections.h2: What is Livingston's history and layout?
sections.html:
Settlers from Newark negotiated for the Horseneck Tract in 1699, and disputes over land titles led to the Horseneck Riots between 1745 and 1755. Caldwell and Springfield townships each gave up land when the township was chartered on February 5, 1813, and William Livingston, New Jersey's first governor, is its namesake. Fairmount (now part of West Orange) split off in 1862 and Roseland in 1908.

The town grew slowly until automobiles arrived. Mount Pleasant Avenue, one of the first turnpikes in the state, was once the main access. The population rose from 5,972 in 1940 to 23,124 in 1960 and peaked near 30,127 in 1970 before settling in the 26,000 to 28,000 range, then climbing back to 31,330 by 2020.

Livingston sits in southwestern Essex County, bordered by Roseland to the north, West Orange to the east, Millburn and Short Hills to the south, and Florham Park and East Hanover in Morris County to the west. The Passaic River marks the western edge. Place names buyers use include Cheapside, Northfield, Washington Place, West Livingston and Cedar Ridge.

sections.h2: How expensive are Livingston homes compared with local incomes?
sections.html:
Owners live in 88.9% of Livingston homes, and the middle owned home is worth $821,100. At that value a typical sale reaches one of the upper brackets of the state fee schedule.

sections.h2: How do schools, hospitals and parks affect Livingston homes?
sections.html:
Schools are the first filter for most buyers. Livingston Public Schools have six elementary schools (Burnet Hill, Collins, Harrison, Hillside, Mount Pleasant and Riker Hill), Mount Pleasant Middle School for grade 6, Heritage Middle School for grades 7 and 8, and Livingston High School, which received a National Blue Ribbon award in 1997-98. The district had 6,151 students in 2019-20.

Cooperman Barnabas Medical Center, a 597-bed hospital established in 1865, sits in the south of town. More than 470 acres of wooded parkland has hiking trails, and roughly a quarter of the township's land stays in a natural state. Riker Hill Complex is a 204-acre park on the township's edge.

Retail is changing. The Livingston Mall at the southwest corner has lost several anchors, and the Route 10 corridor and the Livingston Avenue center, including the Livingston Town Center mixed-use project, carry more everyday shopping. Office parks along Eisenhower Parkway house companies such as CoreWeave and a Verizon customer service center.

sections.h2: How do residents get to New York and Newark from Livingston?
sections.html:
The township is 21.9 miles from New York City, and rail service runs through stations in neighboring communities. Options buyers compare:

  • Highways: Interstate 280 and Route 10 cross the town, and I-80, the Parkway and the Turnpike are reached via I-280.
  • Bus to Manhattan: the Community Coach 77 line runs to Port Authority in Manhattan, and OurBus operates a commuter route serving Livingston and West Orange.
  • Bus to Newark: NJ Transit routes 70, 71 and 73, with local route 873.
  • Rail: Morristown Line stations in Short Hills, Millburn and South Orange sit 5 to 7 miles away, and the fee-based Livingston Express Shuttle makes a 15-minute run between Livingston Mall and South Orange Station.

sections.h2: Is a C.O. needed to sell in Livingston?
sections.html:
No, the township's FAQ says a C.O. is not required for a sale. It does recommend phoning the Building Department (973-992-5000, extension 5200) to see whether any permits are still open on the property, and to call well ahead of closing because open permits can hold up a sale.

A smoke detector certification is required, and the Livingston Fire Department issues it at 973-992-2373. The department's Fire Prevention Bureau also inspects residential properties at resale or when a rental changes hands, and enforces the state fire code for smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. The Building Department sits at 357 S. Livingston Avenue, second floor.

  • Replacing a sink, toilet or tub in the same spot needs no permit, but moving fixtures does.
  • New electrical or plumbing work needs a permit even when you only swap cabinets.
  • Sheds larger than 200 square feet need a building permit plus zoning approval; smaller ones need zoning approval only.
  • Fences enclosing a pool, spa or hot tub need a building permit.

sections.h2: What fees come due at a Livingston closing?
sections.html:
The seller pays the state's transfer fee when the deed is recorded. At $821,100, a typical Livingston sale reaches the $550,000 to $850,000 band of the over-$350,000 schedule, charged at $5.30 per $500 for that slice, with lower bands applying to the dollars beneath it.

Above $1 million, a graduated fee applies to residential deeds, starting at 1% of the whole price and rising to 3.5% for prices over $3.5 million. The seller is responsible for it, and the deed must carry the state's affidavit form (RTF-1EE). Run the number before you accept an offer close to that line.

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages handles recording for all 22 Essex municipalities, Livingston included, and its record room reaches back to 1637. Confirm the office's current address and hours with the Register before sending documents, or leave it to your closing attorney or title company.

sections.h2: List it or sell it as-is in Livingston?
sections.html:
Where the typical home is worth more than $800,000, a house that is updated and shows well gives a listing room to work. An as-is sale fits better when the house needs a roof, kitchen or systems work, when you have a fixed moving date, or when you inherited the property and want a quick close.

Measure each offer by what you keep. Subtract the transfer fee, repairs a buyer will request, the carrying costs of a listing period and the cost of the smoke certification, and get every offer in writing before you choose.

faqs.q: Does Livingston want a C.O. before a sale?
faqs.a: No, the township says a C.O. is not required. A smoke detector certification from the fire department is, and the Building Department can tell you about open permits, ideally well ahead of closing.

faqs.q: Where do I obtain Livingston's smoke detector certification?
faqs.a: Phone the Livingston Fire Department at 973-992-2373. Its Fire Prevention Bureau covers detector compliance when residential properties are resold.

faqs.q: Is the transfer fee a seller cost in Livingston?
faqs.a: Yes. The state computes it from the price stated in the deed and collects it at recording. Sales above $1 million also carry a graduated percent fee, which the seller owes.

faqs.q: Which office records a Livingston deed?
faqs.a: The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which serves all 22 county municipalities. A closing attorney or title agent usually files the deed.

faqs.q: What if my Livingston house has unpermitted work?
faqs.a: You can still sell, but expect questions. Call the Building Department at 973-992-5000, extension 5200, to learn what is on file; a buyer's lender or attorney may want the work permitted or reflected in the price.
